docs.title: EO Application Packages in 20 minutes
docs.text:
An Earth Observation Application Package (EOAP) describes how to run an EO application: its inputs, outputs, container software and workflow. A compatible runner can use that description to execute the application locally or on a processing platform, close to the data.

This module introduces the idea through one small example: give a GeoTIFF URL to rio bounds and receive a GeoJSON file describing its bounding geometry. You only need to recognise a command line and a URL. No cloud account or software installation is needed for the core lesson.

docs.title: Your 20-minute route
docs.text: Time Activity What you should be able to explain 0–3 min Read this page Why packaging helps others run your application 3–7 min Meet the building blocks How a container, tool and workflow fit together 7–15 min Trace the example How a job input becomes a command and an output 15–18 min Build, deploy and run What the developer and platform each provide 18–20 min Check your understanding Identify the package's interface and portability limits

docs.title: Why learn EOAP in 2026?
docs.text:
ESA's EO Exploitation Platform Common Architecture (EOEPCA) initiative makes application packaging part of a reusable platform architecture. Its evolution, EOEPCA+, develops interoperable building blocks for EO cloud platforms and federation. For students, EOAP is a practical way to describe an application so that those platforms can deploy and execute it. ESA Common Architecture initiative.

  • Deploy and execute: EOEPCA's Processing building block supports OGC Application Packages expressed in CWL and describes execution through a CWL runner on Kubernetes. The package connects the developer's application to the platform's processing services. EOEPCA processing architecture.
  • Develop and share: EOEPCA provides application packaging tools to build container images and describe command-line tools and workflows in CWL. Learning the package's interface prepares you to use these tools and publish your own EO applications. Application package development tools.

These examples show broader use; support still varies between platforms. The OGC Best Practice supplies the common packaging guidance. This lesson uses CWL v1.2 and a typed URI record as a teaching convention.

docs.title: The problem EOAP solves
docs.text:
A script alone leaves questions unanswered: which libraries does it need, how do you pass data, and where are the results? An application package makes those choices explicit. The container supplies the software; CWL describes its invocation and the public interface; a job file supplies values for one run.

For this example:

flowchart LR J[Job: GeoTIFF URI] --> W[Workflow: main] W --> T[Container tool: rio bounds] T --> O[File: bounds.json]

After the lesson, use the optional notebooks to practise writing a CLI, building a container and running a package. The history explains how this approach developed.

Adoption references reviewed on 11 October 2026.

docs.title: Trace an application package · 8 minutes
docs.text: Open quick-start.cwl and inputs.yaml in the repository's notebooks/ directory. The snippets below explain selected parts of those files; they are not complete standalone packages.

docs.title: 1. Find the public interface · 2 minutes
docs.text:
The CWL document declares cwlVersion: v1.2. Its $graph contains a Workflow with id: main and a CommandLineTool with id: rio-bounds.

The workflow accepts geotiff and returns bounds. Its input uses a record type named URI, imported from the shared EOAP schemas:

geotiff:
  type: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eoap/schemas/main/string_format.yaml#URI
  label: GeoTIFF URI
  doc: URI of the GeoTIFF whose bounding geometry will be returned.

The record has one string field, value. It comes from the remote string_format.yaml schema imported by both the workflow and tool:

SchemaDefRequirement:
  types:
    - $import: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eoap/schemas/main/string_format.yaml

This shared URI convention is also used in the mastering-app-package module; it is not a built-in CWL type or a universal requirement for every EOAP. Resolving the package requires access to the remote schema. Native File and Directory types have different staging semantics: the runner manages files or directories, whereas this tool reads the URI itself.

docs.title: 2. Supply a value · 2 minutes
docs.text:
The job file contains:

geotiff:
  value: https://sentinel-cogs.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/sentinel-s2-l2a-cogs/10/T/FK/2021/7/S2B_10TFK_20210713_0_L2A/B02.tif

The nesting matters: geotiff receives a record containing value, not a bare URL string. The package also has a default GeoTIFF URI, so a job file can be omitted for the default run.

Try it on paper: change B02.tif to B01.tif in a copy of the job. Which file describes the new execution? The job file; the application package stays the same.

docs.title: 3. Follow the command and output · 3 minutes
docs.text:
The workflow connects its input to the tool:

steps:
  bounds:
    run: '#rio-bounds'
    in:
      geotiff: geotiff
    out: [bounds]

The tool uses baseCommand: rio and arguments: [bounds]. Its binding extracts the URL:

inputBinding:
  position: 1
  valueFrom: $(self.value)

Together these construct rio bounds <GeoTIFF-URL>. The tool's stdout: bounds.json captures the command's output. Its outputBinding.glob: bounds.json collects that file, and the workflow's outputSource: bounds/bounds exposes it to the caller.

The result is GeoJSON describing the raster's bounding geometry. This example reads raster metadata; it does not produce a cropped raster. The cropping notebooks are a separate, longer exercise.

docs.title: 4. Identify the environment · 1 minute
docs.text:
Find DockerRequirement.dockerPull, NetworkAccess and the s: metadata in the complete file. The image supplies rio; network access allows the remote GeoTIFF to be read; metadata identifies the application, author, version, license and documentation.

The image localhost/rio:latest is built locally for this lesson. A shared deployment needs an image reference the target platform can retrieve, preferably pinned to a digest.

Continue to build, deploy and run, then return for the final two-minute check.

docs.title: Check your understanding
docs.text:
Answer without running anything:

  1. Which class exposes the application's public inputs and outputs?
  2. What command runs when geotiff.value is supplied?
  3. How does bounds.json become a workflow result?
  4. Can a cloud platform retrieve an image built only on your laptop?
Check your answers
  1. The Workflow named main.
  2. rio bounds <the supplied URL> inside the selected container.
  3. stdout creates it, the tool collects it with glob, and the workflow exposes it through outputSource.
  4. The platform needs an accessible registry image or an explicitly supported image-loading mechanism.

You have finished the core lesson when you can explain input → workflow → container command → output and name one platform dependency.

docs.title: Optional: execute the example after the lesson
docs.text:
Allow extra time for installation, image download and network access. You need cwltool, Podman and access to the sample GeoTIFF. In a terminal, start at the repository root:

cd notebooks
cwltool --validate quick-start.cwl

Build the lesson image from a separate Dockerfile; the tracked notebooks/Dockerfile is a different GDAL-based example:

cat > Dockerfile.rio <<'EOF'
FROM docker.io/python:3.12-slim
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends libexpat1 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir rasterio==1.5.1 click==8.4.1
ENTRYPOINT []
EOF
podman build -t localhost/rio:latest -f Dockerfile.rio .
cwltool --podman --outdir results quick-start.cwl inputs.yaml

A successful run reports the bounds output and writes results/bounds.json. Inspect that file for GeoJSON geometry. Image failures usually indicate a missing local image; remote-read failures require checking the URL and network access.

For further practice, open 01 Command line, 02 Container, then 03 Package. These are optional labs outside the 20-minute route.

docs.title: Build, deploy and run · 3 minutes
docs.text:
The same package can support local testing and platform execution. The surrounding services depend on the platform.

Phase Application developer or user Runner or platform Build Write a CLI, build its image, describe the interface in CWL, validate and test Execute a test job with a CWL runner Deploy Publish accessible artifacts and request onboarding Check package support, permissions, image policy and resources Run Supply input values and request execution Resolve data access, schedule tools, monitor the job and return outputs

docs.title: Local execution
docs.text: A CWL runner such as cwltool reads the package and job values, starts the container and collects declared outputs. In this lesson the tool reads a remote GeoTIFF directly. Other applications may require input downloads or output uploads, often called stage-in and stage-out.

docs.title: Platform execution in 2026
docs.text:
OGC API — Processes can expose a packaged application as a service: clients discover its interface, submit jobs and retrieve results. Deployment requires the platform's supported onboarding mechanism; an execution API alone does not imply arbitrary package deployment. The OGC EOAP Best Practice describes the package-to-process mapping.

ESA's EOEPCA initiative supplies reusable platform building blocks for this lifecycle. Its Processing architecture describes deployment of OGC Application Packages and execution of their CWL workflows, with a runner handling computation on Kubernetes. This connects the package you write to a platform service that schedules work and manages results. EOEPCA processing architecture.

docs.title: What remains platform-specific?
docs.text:
The package describes computation. The deployment supplies identity, credentials, storage, scheduling and quotas. For a remote deployment, check that the image is accessible, data references can be resolved, required CWL features are supported and resource requests fit the platform.

Discuss: your package runs locally but fails on another platform. If its image exists only as localhost/rio:latest, what needs to change? Publish the image to an accessible registry and update the package reference before investigating the processing logic.

Finish with the two-minute knowledge check.

docs.title: YAML: a one-minute reference
docs.text: CWL packages and job files in this module use YAML. You only need three structures to read the example.

docs.title: Values and maps
docs.text:
Write key: value, with a space after the colon. Indentation nests values under a parent key; use spaces, not tabs.

geotiff:
  value: https://example.org/image.tif

Here geotiff is a map containing a value string. This matches the lesson's URI record input. A bare geotiff: https://example.org/image.tif would have a different type.

docs.title: Lists
docs.text:
A dash introduces a list item. Brackets are a compact alternative:

arguments:
  - bounds
# Equivalent: arguments: [bounds]

The package's $graph is a list of process descriptions, including the workflow and tool.

docs.title: Quotes and comments
docs.text:
Quote values when punctuation or an intended string type could be ambiguous. In particular, quote a fragment such as '#URI': an unquoted # following whitespace starts a comment.

cwlVersion: v1.2
input_type: '#URI'  # A schema reference represented as a string
version_label: '1.0.0'

true is a boolean and 42 is a number; '42' is a string. Preserve the type expected by the CWL input.

Return to the example. See the YAML specification for the full syntax.

docs.title: The EO Applications Pilot · historical context
docs.text:
This page describes the origins of EOAP. For current adoption and the introductory lesson, start with EOAP in 20 minutes.

The OGC Innovation Program's Earth Observation Applications Pilot, conducted between December 2019 and July 2020, investigated the software architecture initially developed through OGC Testbeds 13-15. This architecture facilitated the deployment and execution of externally developed applications on Earth Observation (EO) data and processing platforms.

The pilot program served as an evaluation of the interoperability frameworks previously established in OGC Testbeds 13 to 15, proving to be a foundational step for conducting maturity assessments within operational environments. During the pilot, further enhancements and precise definitions were crafted, which refined the process for deploying and executing applications across a variety of platforms with only minimal modifications required.

The Pilot validated the strategy of using Docker for secure and efficient application packaging, and HTTP Web APIs or Web Services for managing and executing applications. Moreover, the pilot defined clear application patterns that govern data inputs and outputs, reinforced the use of the Common Workflow Language (CWL) for detailed application description, execution, and workflow construction. It also endorsed the adoption of the SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog (STAC) to serve as a comprehensive data manifest, delineating the necessary inputs and outputs for applications. These advancements collectively enhance the deployment flexibility and interoperability of applications within diverse EO data ecosystems.

The conclusion of the OGC Earth Observation Applications Pilot emphasized the need for standardized subsets of the Common Workflow Language (CWL) that all platforms should support. This standardization was reckoned essential to ensure that application developers experience consistency and predictability when deploying their applications across different platforms. As a result, the pilot advocated for the creation of an OGC Best Practice document that would outline the use of CWL within application packages.

This proposed Best Practice document would aim to serve as a comprehensive guide, addressing the diverse application design patterns explored during the pilot. It would provide detailed guidelines for the automated generation of CWL, enabling a more streamlined and efficient development process for EO applications. This initiative would seek to enhance the interoperability and usability of Earth Observation data and processing platforms by leveraging CWL’s robust framework for describing and executing workflows, thereby fostering a more unified and effective approach to application development within the geospatial community.

docs.title: From pilots to wider use
docs.text:
This history is optional reading after the 20-minute lesson.

OGC Testbeds 13–15 explored application deployment near EO data. The 2019–2020 EO Applications Pilot tested interoperability between providers and informed the Best Practice for Earth Observation Application Package. The published best practice remains the reference for this module. OGC Best Practice.

By 2026, introductory teaching should also cover ESA's EOEPCA initiative and its evolution, EOEPCA+. The initiative develops interoperable building blocks for EO platforms and federation; its Processing architecture supports OGC Application Packages expressed in CWL. This gives students a concrete path from the early packaging experiments to reusable platform services. Support and onboarding requirements still depend on the deployment. ESA Common Architecture initiative, EOEPCA processing architecture.

For the earlier architecture, read previous OGC testbeds, the EO Applications Pilot and the published best practice. Historical references to WPS, EMS and ADES describe that period; present deployments may expose different services and onboarding paths.

docs.title: The published OGC Best Practice
docs.text:
The OGC Best Practice for Earth Observation Application Package, 20-089r1 documents how to package EO applications using a command-line interface, container software and CWL workflow descriptions. It also covers metadata, application patterns and platform responsibilities.

It is a published best-practice document, not a guarantee that an arbitrary package runs on every platform. A deployment needs compatible CWL features, accessible software and data, and appropriate runtime resources.

For this module, first learn to identify the workflow interface, tool bindings, container reference and outputs in the example. Consult the original document when you need exact requirement wording or guidance for a production package.

docs.title: Previous OGC testbeds · historical context
docs.text:
This page describes the origins of EOAP. For current adoption and the introductory lesson, start with EOAP in 20 minutes.

The OGC initiatives in Testbed-13, Testbed-14, and Testbed-15 have pioneered the development of an advanced architectural framework designed to facilitate the ad-hoc deployment and execution of applications proximate to the data source. This strategic positioning minimizes data transfer, enhancing efficiency between data repositories and application processes.

These testbeds laid the foundational design for an architecture that supports the encapsulation, deployment, and execution of Earth Observation Applications across distributed Cloud Platforms. This framework ensures that applications are efficiently integrated and managed within cloud environments, providing scalable solutions for Earth Observation data processing.

Building on established OGC standards such as WPS (Web Processing Service) and OWS-Context, these testbed activities have refined the concept of Application Packages. These packages encapsulate data processing applications or workflows, allowing for streamlined deployment and execution across varied Cloud Platforms.

The WPS service plays a pivotal role by enabling end-user portals and B2B client applications to submit processing parameters, initiate on-demand or systematic data processing requests, and establish data pipelines for retrieving the processed information.

Each Application Package contains detailed specifications about the execution units or workflow scripts to be executed, along with configurations for parameterization or customization. This modular approach facilitates the precise tailoring of processing workflows to specific project needs.

The architecture articulated in these testbeds integrates the Application Package with key services: the Execution Management Service (EMS) and the Application Deployment and Execution Service (ADES). The EMS orchestrates the deployment and invocation of processing services workflows, leveraging multiple deployment and execution platforms through WPS-T, a transactional extension of WPS. The ADES, in turn, functions as the execution engine, managing the application lifecycle previously configured as a WPS service by the EMS.

The EMS orchestrates the application package across the selected ADES platform, managing the deployment and execution of workflow components either locally or remotely. It ensures a streamlined operation from deployment to execution, fostering a responsive and agile processing environment.

Primary responsibilities of the ADES include:

  • Validating and approving application deployment and execution requests from the EMS.
  • Managing the execution of processes within the processing cluster, ensuring robust performance and reliability.
  • Monitoring ongoing process execution to maintain operational integrity and performance.
  • Retrieving and delivering processed results efficiently, ensuring data integrity and accessibility.

Additionally, the ADES handles critical sub-steps such as the staging-in of input data and the staging-out of output data, essential for maintaining a seamless flow in data processing activities. This comprehensive approach not only enhances operational efficiency but also ensures that the architecture can support complex, data-intensive workflows in an optimized manner.

docs.title: Prepare the application
docs.text: This is an optional reference after the 20-minute introduction. Start with a command that accepts explicit arguments, runs without prompts, returns a failure status on errors and writes outputs to its working directory.

docs.title: Bundle its software
docs.text:
A container image includes the executable and its runtime dependencies. The container notebook uses Python 3.12, pinned Python dependencies and the native libexpat1 library needed by its rasterio environment:

FROM docker.io/python:3.12-slim
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends libexpat1 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir rasterio==1.5.1 click==8.4.1 pystac==1.15.2 loguru==0.7.3 pyproj==3.7.2 shapely==2.1.2 && python -c "import rasterio"
ADD app.py /app/app.py
ENTRYPOINT []

The notebook creates app.py before building this image. This cropping application is distinct from the smaller rio bounds example.

docs.title: Make execution repeatable
docs.text:
Use explicit inputs, write results under the current working directory and avoid relying on host-specific paths. Test with the intended user permissions. Publish shared images to an accessible registry and record an image digest for reproducible releases. Supply data credentials through the execution environment rather than embedding them in an image.

Practise with 01 Command line and 02 Container. For the normative command-line, container and registry requirements, read the OGC Best Practice.

docs.title: Prepare the package
docs.text: This is an optional reference after the 20-minute introduction. Use the repository's complete example as the starting point, rather than copying incomplete fragments.

docs.title: Describe the interface
docs.text:
Use CWL v1.2 for this module. Declare a workflow entrypoint and the tools it invokes. Give processes, steps, inputs and outputs meaningful identifiers, labels and descriptions. Define types deliberately: native File and Directory inputs support runner-managed staging; the example's imported URI record lets its tool read a URL directly.

Connect workflow inputs to step inputs and declare output sources. On each tool, specify the command, argument bindings, container and output collection. Declare required network, expression and resource capabilities where applicable. A workflow may have one step or several; add scatter requirements when a design uses scattering.

docs.title: Identify the application
docs.text: The example uses the s: https://schema.org/ namespace to record name, description, software version, repository, creation date, license, author, publisher and documentation. Port descriptions explain the interface; application metadata supports discovery and attribution. A validator's metadata profile can impose additional conventions beyond CWL syntax.

docs.title: Validate, then execute
docs.text:
From the repository root, in an environment with the dependencies installed:

cwltool --validate notebooks/quick-start.cwl
python scripts/cwl-docs.py --validate

The helper checks this repository's metadata and description conventions, validates with cwltool, and renders Markdown under /tmp/stac-cwl-docs by default. It is not an EOAP conformance validator. An EOAP validator additionally checks package structure and applicable best-practice rules; check which profiles it reports.

Validation does not prove that an image can be retrieved or an algorithm produces correct results. Run a representative job and inspect its output, then test the target platform's data access and resource requirements.

Practise with 03 Package. The OGC Best Practice is the authoritative reference for requirement wording; the CWL specifications define execution semantics.

docs.title: How CWL fits EOAP
docs.text:
The OGC Best Practice for Earth Observation Application Package uses CWL to describe an application interface, its workflow and the containerised tools it invokes.

The Workflow supplies the public application interface. CommandLineTool descriptions supply commands, argument bindings and container requirements. A platform can use that interface to describe a remotely callable process, while a local CWL runner can execute the same computation with a job file.

CWL is a general workflow language used beyond Earth Observation. EOAP adds EO packaging guidance, metadata and data handling patterns. STAC can describe input and output data assets in those patterns; the lesson's small raster-bounds example simply accepts a GeoTIFF URI and returns a file.

Start with the building blocks and the guided example. For wider workflows, explore the community's application package patterns.

docs.title: The building blocks · 4 minutes
docs.text: The Common Workflow Language (CWL) describes tools and workflows in a form that a runner can interpret. It separates an application's interface from the machine that executes it. This module uses CWL v1.2; consult the CWL specifications for the complete language.

docs.title: Four things to recognise
docs.text:
Building block Responsibility In our example Container image Supplies executable software and libraries Rasterio and its rio command CommandLineTool Maps typed inputs to a command and collects files rio bounds <URL> → bounds.json Workflow Exposes the application interface and connects steps main runs the rio-bounds tool Job file Supplies values for one execution geotiff.value contains a GeoTIFF URL

A workflow can have one step. It provides a stable public interface even when the implementation later grows to several steps.

docs.title: Read the execution contract
docs.text:
inputs and outputs declare names and types. inputBinding tells the runner how to construct arguments. outputBinding.glob tells it which files to collect. A tool runs in its own working directory; write results there so the runner can retrieve them.

requirements state capabilities needed to execute the tool. In our example, DockerRequirement selects the image, NetworkAccess permits remote data access, and SchemaDefRequirement imports the shared URI schema. InlineJavascriptRequirement permits the expression that extracts the URL from that record. A requirement must be supported; a hint is optional advice to a runner.

docs.title: What travels with the package?
docs.text:
The CWL document contains the interface, workflow, software references and metadata. Container images are separate artifacts referenced by the document. Job values are separate too, so you can process different data without rewriting the package.

Portability depends on a compatible runner, accessible images, data permissions and sufficient resources. A container helps reproduce the software environment; recording image digests, input versions and parameters helps reproduce a result.

Continue to trace the raster-bounds example. If YAML is unfamiliar, take the one-minute syntax reference alongside it.
